Top.deeper: Top-making turns scoured wool into a parallel, even strand in several steps: carding opens the fiber into a web and sliver, gill boxes with pinned fallers draft and align it, combing removes short fibers, neps and remaining vegetable matter as noil, and finisher gilling evens the combed sliver before it is wound into balls or bumps. Because top is the point at which wool is most often traded internationally after scouring, it is also a measurement point: mean fiber diameter of combed sliver is measured by airflow under IWTO-6, and the Laserscan (IWTO-12) and OFDA (IWTO-47) methods report the diameter distribution as well as the mean. Those diameters underpin fineness designations such as Super 100s, which corresponds to about 18.75 microns under the IWTO code. Top is also a common point for dyeing, for wool and for dehaired cashmere, which is often dyed as loose stock or top.
Top.origins: Fine wool is traded in three stages, greasy fleece, scoured wool and combed top, and top-making often sits with specialized processors rather than spinners. Its certification history tracks instrument development: in 1995 IWTO accepted both the Laserscan and OFDA methods for raw wool and top certification, which made routine reporting of diameter variability practical alongside the mean micron figure.

Traceability.deeper: Traceability can rest on documents, on markers added to the product, or on properties measured in the material itself. Documentary systems link purchases, batches and transaction certificates. Added markers include producer tracers, such as the FiberPrint additive that Unifi states lets its REPREVE content be detected later. Intrinsic fingerprints are an active research area: a 2026 study measured 21 mineral elements by ICP-MS in 237 cashmere samples from three regions of Inner Mongolia (Ordos, Chifeng and Alxa League) and four breeds, and identified six elements (magnesium, manganese, arsenic, strontium, cerium and uranium) that discriminated origin, with regional classification more accurate than breed. Species identity is a separate question answered by microscopy, DNA or proteomics. Some claims cannot be tested in the fiber at all: recycled and virgin PET, or lyocell from recycled and wood pulp, are chemically identical, so origin depends on records.
Traceability.origins: Labeling law reaches only part of the chain. The US Textile Fiber Products Identification Act, approved on 2 September 1958, requires the generic fiber names and the country where the product was processed or manufactured, not where the fiber was grown. Traceability as a sourcing discipline grew beyond that baseline as buyers asked for farm, gin, mill and dyehouse links, and as certification schemes added shipment-level records. Claims such as Pima, Egyptian or organic cannot be confirmed by routine fiber tests and depend on documentation.

Warp & weft.deeper: The two systems face different mechanical demands. Warp yarns are held under tension through the whole weaving process and abraded by heddles and reed, so they are commonly given more twist and protected with size that is later removed in desizing; typical cotton twist multipliers are about 3.8 to 4.5 for warp yarns against about 3.0 to 3.6 for weft and knitting yarns. Density is counted separately as ends per unit width in the warp and picks per unit length in the weft, and the warp is set through a reed with a fixed number of dents. Interlacing makes each system bend around the other, and the resulting crimp differs between directions, one reason fabrics stretch and shrink differently lengthwise and crosswise. Denim shows the separation clearly: indigo is applied to the warp by repeated dipping and oxidation, producing ring-dyed yarn, while the weft often stays undyed.
Warp & weft.origins: The vocabulary follows the loom. Warp names the yarns set up first and held under tension; weft, also called filling in US mill usage, names the yarn laid across them pick by pick. Because warp ends must pass through a reed, recording ends per inch is intrinsic to weaving, and the later retail thread-count figure simply adds ends and picks. Weave names describe how the two systems interlace, from the two-shed plain weave to twills needing at least three shafts.

Weaving.deeper: A loom repeats three primary motions: shedding, which lifts selected warp ends to open a gap; picking, which inserts weft through the shed; and beating-up, in which the reed pushes the new pick against the cloth, while let-off and take-up keep warp tension and advance the fabric. The interlacing plan sets the float length. Plain weave, written 1/1, has the shortest floats and highest crimp; twills need at least three sheds and satins at least five. Experimental comparisons of plain, 2/2 twill and eight-end satin fabrics woven from the same yarns report measurable differences in stiffness and tensile behavior, with float length identified as a controlling factor. Compactness has environmental effects as well: in one laundering study, woven polyester shed about 17 fibers per square centimeter against about 24 for a knit, and alkali treatment cut woven shedding by up to 89.6 percent.
Weaving.origins: Weave complexity tracks loom capability. Plain weave needs only two alternating sheds, so it can be produced on the simplest looms, which explains why many unrelated weaving traditions and so many fabric names distinguished by fiber and finish, from calico to taffeta. Twills required a third shaft, and satins demanded more shafts or a figure-harness mechanism; the extra control produced families of named fabrics such as drill, serge, gabardine and denim.

Worsted.deeper: The worsted system aims for parallel fibers and a compact, smooth yarn. Scoured wool is carded, gilled on pinned fallers, combed to remove noil and made into top; the top is then drawn and gilled down through further stages to roving and spun, usually with enough twist to bind the aligned fibers. The woollen system instead condenses carded fiber and spins it directly, keeping fibers less parallel for bulky, lofty yarn. Worsted yarns have their own traditional count, the number of 560-yard hanks per pound, so tex is roughly 886 divided by the worsted count. Fineness grading is tied to the worsted tradition: under the IWTO code Super 100s corresponds to about 18.75 microns mean diameter, and each further step of 10 is about 0.5 micron finer. Finer fibers allow more fibers per yarn cross-section at a given count, permitting finer yarns and lighter cloth.
Worsted.origins: The name comes from Worstead, a village in Norfolk, England, long associated with a smooth cloth woven from combed wool. Over time worsted came to name the whole combed-wool processing route rather than a single cloth, while woollen named the carded route. The Super S numbers used on worsted suitings are generally described as descending from the older worsted quality-number tradition, in which finer wool could be spun to higher counts.
